title: Advantages, Limitations, and Alternatives
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of advantages, limitations, and alternatives and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to advantages, limitations, and alternatives.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on advantages, limitations, and alternatives. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: GitHub-hosted runners reduce machine maintenance, while self-hosted runners add control but require stronger isolation, patching, access controls, and cost monitoring. Treat the workflow as an event-driven automation graph: an event starts the run, jobs are scheduled, steps execute on runners, and the run records a result. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Benefits and trade-offs of workflow automation
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: GitHub-hosted versus self-hosted execution
items.text: Choose runner labels and access boundaries that match the workload. Self-hosted machines need patching, network segmentation, secret protection, and cleanup; keep untrusted contributions away from privileged persistent runners.

items.title: When external CI/CD systems may be appropriate
items.text: For when external ci/cd systems may be appropriate, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Runtime, resource, access, and cost considerations
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

content_blocks.code:
name: Validate workflow configuration
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "Replace with a real validation command"
content_blocks.expected_output: A push or pull request starts a read-only job; replace the demonstration command with a check appropriate to the repository.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a test repository or static validation first. Confirm the snippet matches the repository, runner, permissions, and current GitHub documentation.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Remove temporary test workflows and never carry test credentials or sample outputs into production.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to advantages, limitations, and alternatives. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain advantages, limitations, and alternatives, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Understand why automation belongs beside source control and how events become repeatable work.

content.task: Apply advantages, limitations, and alternatives to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: GitHub-hosted runners reduce machine maintenance, while self-hosted runners add control but require stronger isolation, patching, access controls, and cost monitoring.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: GitHub-hosted runners reduce machine maintenance, while self-hosted runners add control but require stronger isolation, patching, access controls, and cost monitoring. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: GitHub-hosted runners reduce machine maintenance, while self-hosted runners add control but require stronger isolation, patching, access controls, and cost monitoring.
Treat the workflow as an event-driven automation graph: an event starts the run, jobs are scheduled, steps execute on runners, and the run records a result.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
